content: Ascites refers to the pathological accumulation of fluid within the abdominal cavity. This condition is frequently observed in women with advanced ovarian cancer and, to a lesser extent, in those with advanced endometrial cancer. These patients often require repeated drainage procedures to manage the ascites. However, the guidelines that inform the management of ascites drainage are typically developed at a local level and are not based on robust evidence. Optimizing the management of drainage procedures is critical, as it has the potential to enhance the efficacy of the intervention and improve the quality of life (QoL) for women during this challenging phase of their illness. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and potential adverse events associated with various interventions for the management of malignant ascites drainage in women with gynaecological cancers receiving palliative care. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, up to November 4, 2019. Additional sources, such as clinical trial registries, grey literature, conference reports, citation lists, and key textbooks, were also reviewed to identify relevant studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving women with malignant ascites secondary to gynaecological cancers. If studies included participants with non-gynaecological cancers, data specific to women with gynaecological cancers were extracted or requested from the trial authors. If this was not feasible, studies were included only if at least 50% of the participants had gynaecological cancers. Two independent reviewers selected the studies, extracted data, assessed the quality of the included studies, and evaluated the certainty of the evidence using Cochrane methodology. In the original 2010 review, no relevant studies were identified. However, in this updated review, one RCT involving 245 participants was included. This trial compared two interventions: abdominal paracentesis combined with intraperitoneal infusion of catumaxomab versus abdominal paracentesis alone. The study was determined to have a high risk of bias across nearly all domains, and the data were deemed unsuitable for robust analysis. The results indicated that the median time to the first deterioration in QoL ranged from 19 to 26 days in participants who underwent paracentesis alone, compared to 47 to 49 days in those who received paracentesis with catumaxomab infusion. However, this evidence was of very low certainty. Adverse events were reported exclusively in the group receiving catumaxomab infusion, with the most common severe adverse events being abdominal pain and lymphopenia. These findings were also based on very low-certainty evidence. Importantly, no data were available regarding symptom improvement, participant and caregiver satisfaction, or cost-effectiveness. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend the most effective approach for managing malignant ascites drainage in women with gynaecological cancers. The findings from the single included RCT, which was small and at high risk of bias, provide very low-certainty evidence. Further high-quality research is urgently needed to guide clinical practice in this area.
